title.value: Protecting Label Distribution in Cross-Silo Federated Learning
Protecting Label Distribution in Cross-Silo Federated Learning

abstract.value: Federated learning (FL) is a popular distributed machine learning (ML) framework in which multiple parties share their model parameters instead of the raw training datasets to construct a global model in a privacy-preserving manner. However, existing FL solutions mainly focus on protecting the privacy of individual training records by incorporating differential privacy (DP), while overlooking the protection of the distribution information of training datasets, despite the fact that data distribution is also regarded as highly sensitive in high-stakes applications. In this paper, we propose the first privacy-preserving stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm for protecting label distribution in FL. To establish a formal privacy guarantee, we formalize a privacy notion, dubbed (m, γ, ξ)-label distributional privacy, to quantify label distributional privacy leakage. Subsequently, we design the label distribution perturbation mechanism (LDPM) that carefully incorporates randomness into the SGD algorithm to achieve (m, γ, ξ)-label distributional privacy for all one-vs-all classification models. LDPM is easy to implement and provides non-trivial privacy guarantees, making it a suitable drop-in replacement for existing FL local model training algorithms. Notably, we demonstrate that LDPM also ensures DP, indicating that LDPM offers both individual and label distributional privacy guarantees. Extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of LDPM. 4828 2024 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

Federated learning (FL) is a popular distributed ma- chine learning (ML) framework in which multiple parties share their model parameters instead of the raw training datasets to construct a global model in a privacy-preserving manner. However, existing FL solutions mainly focus on protecting the privacy of individual training records by incorporating differential privacy (DP), while overlooking the protection of the distribution information of training datasets, despite the fact that data distribution is also regarded as highly sensitive in high-stakes applications. In this paper, we propose the first privacy-preserving stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm for protecting la- bel distribution in FL. To establish a formal privacy guarantee, we formalize a privacy notion, dubbed (m, γ, ξ)-label distribu- tional privacy, to quantify label distributional privacy leakage. Subsequently, we design the label distribution perturbation mechanism (LDPM) that carefully incorporates randomness into the SGD algorithm to achieve (m, γ, ξ)-label distributional privacy for all one-vs-all classification models. LDPM is easy to implement and provides non-trivial privacy guarantees, mak- ing it a suitable drop-in replacement for existing FL local model training algorithms. Notably, we demonstrate that LDPM also ensures DP, indicating that LDPM offers both individual and label distributional privacy guarantees. Extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of LDPM. 1. Introduction Federated learning (FL) [ 1]-[3] has become a promis- ing privacy-preserving framework for distributed machine learning (ML), in which multiple parties first train local models on their local data, then iteratively share their local model parameters with a server to build a global model that provides a better model utility than individual local models. Since parties never disclose their local data to other entities, FL provides a higher level of privacy protection compared to traditional centralized ML in which all local datasets are transmitted to a trusted party for model training. However, existing work [ 4]-[6] has demonstrated that the adversary can still infer sensitive information about local training datasets from local model parameters because of the memorization nature of ML models [ 7]. To further protect data privacy for FL parties, recent studies [ 8]-[10] propose to incorporate differential privacy (DP) [ 11], [ 12] into each party's local training process: local parties first perturb their plain model parameters by a DP mechanism and then submit the perturbed parameters to the server, which can significantly reduce the adversaries' ability to extract sensitive information from the submitted parameters. Nevertheless, the theoretical privacy guarantee offered by DP applies to individual records (e.g., the feature values of a particular record) rather than aggregate statistics of datasets (e.g., label distribution). In particular, as we shall discuss in Section 2.2, the privacy guarantee of DP for the distribution information can be quite weak, especially when the size of the input dataset is large. 1.1. Motivation In many practical scenarios, the distribution information of parties' local datasets is deemed confidential. Businesses often view their aggregate statistics as proprietary infor- mation; unauthorized disclosure of such data can cause substantial harm to the data owners. This type of privacy leakage is particularly problematic in cross-silo FL, where parties are typically commercial companies or organizations managing large quantities of training data. For example, consider the scenario where multiple commercial banks jointly perform an FL task to build an anti-fraud model. If the data distribution information (e.g., income or age distribution) about a bank's customer base is disclosed, adversaries (e.g., competing financial institutions) can use leaked data distributions to devise strategies aimed at the corresponding user groups, potentially snatching customers from the FL party. Furthermore, the leaked data distributions can be utilized by an adversary to boost the accuracy of membership inference attacks [ 13]. Despite being critical in many high-stakes applications, the protection of data distribution information is seldom con- sidered in current privacy-preserving data analysis frame- works [ 3], [ 14]. In particular, the local datasets of FL parties often contain only partial labels [ 1], [ 15], making it infeasible to balance the labels to mitigate the leakage of label distribution information. While efforts have been made to protect label privacy, existing works [ 16], [ 17] mainly focus on protecting indi- vidual records' label information while failing to offer any level of vanilla DP guarantees. It is of particular importance for data analytic tasks to, at the very least, ensure individual- level privacy, as any disclosure of personal data could lead to a direct violation of privacy regulations such as GDPR [ 18] and CCPA [ 19]. Furthermore, these mechanisms are based 4828 DOI 10.1109/SP54263.2024.00113 on input perturbation (e.g., flipping labels using randomized response [20]), resulting in unnecessary privacy-utility trade- offs for protecting label distribution, making them unsuitable for practical FL applications. As a result, none of the current privacy-preserving solutions manages to provide protection for both individual-level privacy and label distribution in- formation, while maintaining a desirable level of utility. 1.2. Our Contribution Motivated by this, we formalize a notion of privacy, named (m, γ, ξ)-label distributional privacy, to quantify the label distribution information leakage. This notion can be framed as a group extension of label DP [17], hence it satisfies two fundamental privacy properties [21], [22] - convexity and transformation invariance. Roughly speaking, a randomized mechanism M satisfies (m, γ, ξ)-label distri- butional privacy, if for any two input datasets of the same size but differing by m labels, the output of M should have “indistinguishable” distributions. Intuitively, when m becomes proportional to the size of the input dataset, this privacy notion ensures that an adversary can hardly infer the label distribution of input datasets accurately by only observing the output of M. Building on the notion of label distributional privacy, we design the Label Distribution Perturbation Mechanism (LDPM), a variant of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm, that satisfies (m, γ, ξ)-label distributional privacy to mitigate the label distribution information leakage in FL. It is important to note that while this privacy notion is a direct group extension of label DP, it brings two significant challenges in algorithm designs: (i) maintaining meaningful model utility while ensuring privacy guarantees, i.e., inject- ing noise as minimally as possible, and (ii) analyzing the privacy cost given that the output distribution of LDPM is rather complicated. To tackle the first challenge, we examine how the gradients behave under identical features but different labels. Based on observations of the shape of gradient difference, we propose a gradient perturbation- based mechanism that carefully introduces randomness into the gradients to protect the label distribution. Our key insight is that altering the label of one record only leads to a change in a small dimension of the gradient. In other words, only a small portion of the gradient elements would leak sensitive label information about input records. Leveraging this characteristic, we inject carefully tailored noise into the gradients to shield label distribution information. To analyze the privacy cost, we derive the closed-form privacy bound by examining the R ´enyi divergence between two nested mixtures of high-dimensional Gaussians. Notably, our privacy analysis holds for all one-vs-all classification models - models that divide the multi-class classification problem into several binary classification problems [23], including widely adopted models such as logistic regression (LR) and support vector machine (SVM). We further demonstrate that LDPM also offers a privacy guarantee in terms of vanilla DP, and thus, it ensures both individual and label distributional privacy guarantees for FL parties. Unlike the group extensions of existing label privacy mechanisms, LDPM provides both group label DP and vanilla DP guarantees. This fundamental distinction sets LDPM apart from all existing label DP algorithms. It is also noteworthy that LDPM is easy to implement and compatible with existing Byzantine-robust FL algorithms [24]-[26], as these algorithms modify the FL aggregation rule from the server's side while keeping the local training process unchanged. These features render LDPM a direct drop-in replacement for the existing FL local model training algorithms, offering an extra layer of privacy protection. Extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets demon- strate that LDPM can effectively mitigate label distribution leakage in FL while keeping desirable model utility. 2. Preliminaries 2.1. Federated Learning Federated averaging (FedAvg) [1] was first proposed by Google and has become one of the most popular frameworks of federated learning (FL) algorithms [3], [27]. In this paper, without loss of generality, we use FedAvg as an example to help illustrate the proposed privacy-preserving mechanism. Let Rf denote the f dimensional input space, and [N] = {1, . . . , N}. Let D = {(x(j), y(j))}j∈[N ] denote a training dataset of N records, where x(j) ∈ X := Rf is the feature of the jth record and y(j) ∈ [c] is the label of x(j). We assume that P (≥ 2) parties participate in FL to collaboratively build a global model, and each party has a local dataset Di (i ∈ [P ]). During each iteration of FL, the parties train their local models based on local training data and then submit their local model parameters to the FL server for aggregation. Let θ(t) i denote the local model parameters submitted by the ith party in the tth iteration, and let Ni denote the number of records in Di. The local model of party i is trained as follows: θ(t) i = arg min θ 1 Ni X (x,y)∈Di ℓ (ψ(x; θ), y) + Ω(θ), where ψ(·; θ) : X 7→ Rc is the model function parame- terized by θ, and it maps an input record x ∈ X into a confidence score vector ˆy ∈ Rc, where the value of the cth element of ˆy is interpreted as the probability that x belongs to the cth class. The loss function ℓ(·, ·) is used to measure the distance between ˆy and the ground truth y. In addition, Ω(·) is a regularization term that mitigates overfitting. After receiving the local models from all parties, the FL server aggregates them into a global model: θ(t) G ← PX i=1 Ni N θ(t) i , where N =PP i=1 Ni is the total number of training records from all parties.
